Not reachable in production yet:
- **No process producer (owner decision 1; blocked on H302).** Nothing in the hub starts run-owned background work and registers its pid: register_process has no caller outside tests. The best first producer is `terminal_run` with `background: true` on the local-host transport. It needs WorkRunLedger.run_for_task; a spawn with start_new_session, bounded log files and a held proc.wait() that records the exit code; a lifetime cap and killpg on cap, ESTOP or stop; a reaper for stopped runs; schema, approval-card and parity updates; and a KillMode in deploy/systemd/jarvis-hub.service (today a restart kills the child and the barrier clears as `exited`, indistinguishable from success). The owner must say whether the task/hook trigger is an accepted adaptation of Hermes's pid/session barrier, or whether a pid wait must be reachable for "equivalent".
- **Pid waits are unusable on macOS/BSD.** There is no start token there, so every pid wait is refused `pid_unprovable`. The fix belongs in exec_cache.py (ctypes libproc proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDTBSDINFO)) or in a producer-held Popen handle, and needs macOS hardware or a macOS CI runner to verify.
- **The judge's `wait` verdict and planner waits are not reachable in production (owner decision 2).** WorkJudge.wait_probe needs a model rubric, and the shipped runtime passes no rubric, model planner or graders. Wiring one needs the owner's choice of local model and provider under H513 (auxiliary_request_scope, strict-local, security.data_training_ack) plus opt-in settings forced off in safe mode. Before any model planner, the rest of the intake arguments must be clamped: since H464c the task's kind is scope-checked as well as Action.kind, but the task's agent, title and payload still reach govern_enqueue unchanged.
- **No graders are wired in production.** After the hub park clears, a run idles until its budget ends. Deterministic verifier and judge adapters belong to the company-mode grading work; they must reuse an existing verdict, because _grade has no try/except and a judge that raises after the verifier recorded leaves `verdict_already_recorded` / `tick_failed` on every later sweep.

Deferred:
- Wake-on-fire: a parked run resumes at the next scheduled sweep.
- A `job:<id>` trigger.
- A process output-pattern trigger (needs the process producer).
- An owner-set wait like Hermes's `/goal wait` (owner decision 3): a clock or own-task wait only, never an owner-typed pid.
- Waiting between checklist steps: the checklist still advances when a step's task is approved, not when it finishes.
- A judge-sourced wait reserves no grading margin (only the hub's park does since H464c), so a judge wait that runs to the end of the budget still leaves the run ungraded. It is reachable only with a judge wait probe (owner decision 2).
- The grading margin bounds one run's way back to a sweep, not a queue: with several runs due at once (max_concurrent 1), a parked run can lose the sweep's one slot after its cap.
- A blocked run whose budget runs out is not settled (H464d settles only runs the sweep skips as budget_spent; a blocked one is skipped as blocked and its resume is refused once the owner answers), so it stays blocked on the record.

Built in #1207 and fixed after six adversarial reviews: review-H465 (one major, seven minors, seven nits), review-H465b (three minors, six nits: a per-turn pass could still run beside /refine and borrow its label, a cut-off review read as nothing, and four mutants were unpinned) and review-H465c (three minors, six nits: a per-turn review cut off by the token cap was refunded, so a model that always truncates reviewed every turn; the settings the replies named could not be set; four survivors) and review-H465d (two minors, seven nits: a day of cut-offs made /refine name the wrong setting, seven real survivors, and a GA4 private key the CLI printed unmasked) and review-H465e (two minors, seven nits: the cut-off refusal on a day of mostly real reviews, nine real survivors, a budget read outside its bounds, a secret echoed by nerva config set, a pass in flight at midnight counted on the next day, a burst of turns past the cadence) and review-H465f (seven nits: a /refine refund keyed on the wrong day, a burst given too few passes, a later bracket closing an unclosed error, a fraction below one read as reviews off). All are fixed. Hermes' /refine [focus] forks the background memory and skill review against a snapshot of the conversation, so the live session is untouched. It refuses while a turn is in flight and reports the new or updated memories and skills back into the chat. Nerva's review engine is the per-turn BackgroundReviewer (strict-local, budgeted); it now also runs on demand.

The command:
- /refine [focus] is an owner command (agents/core/commands.py:395, registered at agents/core/commands.py:665). It answers from any channel's owner, and a guest is refused like any owner command.
- The focus is one line of at most 200 characters.
- It replies with what the review kept, one line per action (profile or core memory updated, corrections recorded, skill patch proposed, new skill quarantined, facts found but not kept because living memory is off). A skill change is said to wait in the Decision Inbox, and a new skill in the pending skills list.
- Every non-run is named: a review already running, the daily budget spent, no local model answering (reviews never leave the machine), a model that spent its whole answer thinking (review_cut_off), a review cut off or malformed (review_unparsed, which names learning.review_max_tokens), reviews switched off (a daily budget of 0, reviews_off), the review outlasting its bound, nothing to review, no reviewer. One refusal added since this row's reviews has no wording of its own: a session whose history was imported from another assistant and is still tainted is refused foreign_history_not_promotable before the lease is looked at (agents/core/orchestrator.py:4272-4273), and the command answers it with the generic "The review did not run." line; the guard came with the owner-attested foreign-history resume (commit 8e1775bb), outside this row's claims and tests. An empty reply, a cut one, or a JSON object carrying none of the review's keys ({} or {"error": …}) is unparsed; only an object that says it found nothing reads as nothing worth keeping. A reply that parses as a review is the model's answer, whatever it opens with or mentions; only a reply that does not parse and is the local degraded message or opens with a bracketed [… error …] closed on its own line by its own bracket is a backend failure; an unclosed "[Note: … error", or one a later [1] or link would close, is prose (review-H465e nit 7, review-H465f nit 3).
- A local backend that is configured but down answers with a degraded string rather than raising. That is no review: it is reported as no local model and costs no budget (review-H465 M-1). A cut-off or malformed /refine costs none either; a per-turn pass cut off the same way does spend its unit, since the model ran to its cap, so the daily budget still bounds local GPU use when a model always truncates, and it is logged at INFO once a day, naming learning.review_max_tokens as the cause of a thinking cut-off and as a possible one of a malformed answer; a /refine cut-off does not use that line up. When such cut-offs are at least half of the day's spent units, /refine answers daily_budget_cut_off and says that, if they were cut off, the token cap is what to raise rather than the budget; one cut-off among real reviews is plain daily_budget (review-H465e m-1). A pass still waiting on the model at midnight refunds or counts against the day it spent its unit on, never the next (review-H465e nit 4), and GET /api/cognition/learning counts cut_offs_today. The unit is spent in run() after the budget is checked again there, so a burst of passes that all saw budget left in should_run cannot pass it; the cadence is checked there again too, so a burst of turns cannot pass it either (review-H465e nit 6), and a pass uses up only the turns that admitted it, so a burst gets the passes the same turns one at a time would (review-H465f nit 2) (_cut_off, agents/core/learning/background_review.py:523).
- It runs whether or not the per-turn learning loop (cognition.review_enabled) is on: the owner asked, as Hermes' manual /refine does.

Orchestrator.refine (agents/core/orchestrator.py:4252):
- It reads a snapshot of the session's history and never writes to it.
- The snapshot is conversation_snapshot (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:98): the newest turns whole and contiguous, each cut at 2,000 characters, up to 12,000 characters in all. Slash commands and the hub's replies to them are left out, so a chat of commands only has nothing to review. This replaces the per-turn review's last-6-turns, 300-character window for this path.
- In flight, as it really behaves: every path that dispatches /refine holds the session's turn lease first. A /refine sent while another turn runs therefore waits for that turn (up to the lease's 180-second bound) and then reviews the conversation as it stands; it is not refused (review-H465 m-1 corrected the earlier claim). The review itself is bounded at 150 seconds (REFINE_TIMEOUT_S), below that wait, so the chat is busy for at most that long.
- A direct caller holding no lease while another turn does is refused turn_in_flight: the lock is locked and the key is not among this context's held leases (agents/core/orchestrator.py:4277). No new in-flight set was added (critic note 1).
- A review's result is the reviewer's last_result, which GET /api/cognition/learning shows (reviewer.status()); a refusal does not overwrite it. Each action is logged.

The learning loop's knobs are declared settings (category learning, agents/core/settings_db.py:350): review_max_tokens (512, 1–32768), review_daily_budget (20, 0–1000), review_cadence (every_turn, every_n_turns, idle_gap), review_every_n (3), review_idle_gap_s (90) and review_max_facts (3), with the defaults the code already used, bounded in _LEARNING_INT_BOUNDS (agents/core/settings_db.py:956). The admin settings API, the HUD and nerva config set can change them; nerva config get shows a number named …max_tokens as the number it is, not masked as a credential, and masks every key the settings store encrypts (the GA4 service-account JSON among them), and nerva config set echoes such a value masked too (review-H465e nit 3). A model id is masked only under a hinted name: llm.default_model shows as typed. Every knob reads within its declared bounds whatever the stored row (a row from before the bounds, restored or hand-edited, reads as the default), the review's model call's token cap included (bounded_learning_int, agents/core/settings_db.py:975). A declared 0 for review_max_facts or review_idle_gap_s is honoured, not read as unset; corrections have a cap of their own (3), so a review_max_facts of 0 keeps no facts, still records corrections, and /refine says what it found but did not keep (_number, agents/core/learning/background_review.py:293).

BackgroundReviewer.run_on_demand (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:335):
- It skips the cadence gate but spends the daily budget, rolling over at midnight, and refunds it when no review was had (a model down, a cut-off answer, a timeout, a cancellation), on the day the pass spent it (review-H465f nit 1). A budget of 0 means no reviews and /refine says so (reviews_off); 2.5 reads as 2, and a value that is not a number or lies outside 0–1000 (text, infinity, a boolean, a hand-edited -3, a fraction below one) is logged once and 20 used (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:268). A per-turn pass that does not run leaves a DEBUG line naming why. It keeps the strict-local model, and is bounded at REFINE_TIMEOUT_S (150 s, below the lease's 180-second wait); no setting raises it.
- It neither resets nor delays the per-turn cadence. It runs one at a time and never beside a per-turn review: a /refine while a per-turn pass runs is refused busy, and a per-turn pass that would start while /refine runs is skipped, not deferred. The exclusion is taken in run() itself (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:394), so a per-turn pass spawned before the /refine, still waiting on the memory lock, is refused on_demand when it enters. A cancelled review leaves no busy flag.
- Its proposals, approval cards and new skills are labelled refine, not background_review; the label is passed down per pass, never kept on the instance. An injection-flagged correction is not recorded (on both paths). Facts found while living memory is off are counted after the injection scan, and said only to the owner who asked.
- run gains a focus slot in REVIEW_PROMPT ("Focus for this review: …", absent when there is none, so the per-turn prompt is byte-identical) and a context bound, which this path sets to the snapshot's.

A cut-off or malformed /refine costs none either; a per-turn pass cut off the same way does spend its unit, since the model ran to its cap, so the daily budget still bounds local GPU use when a model always truncates, and it is logged at INFO once a day, naming learning.review_max_tokens as the cause of a thinking cut-off and as a possible one of a malformed answer; a /refine cut-off does not use that line up. When such cut-offs are at least half of the day's spent units, /refine answers daily_budget_cut_off and says that, if they were cut off, the token cap is what to raise rather than the budget; one cut-off among real reviews is plain daily_budget (review-H465e m-1). A pass still waiting on the model at midnight refunds or counts against the day it spent its unit on, never the next (review-H465e nit 4), and GET /api/cognition/learning counts cut_offs_today. The unit is spent in run() after the budget is checked again there, so a burst of passes that all saw budget left in should_run cannot pass it; the cadence is checked there again too, so a burst of turns cannot pass it either (review-H465e nit 6), and a pass uses up only the turns that admitted it, so a burst gets the passes the same turns one at a time would (review-H465f nit 2) (_cut_off, agents/core/learning/background_review.py:523).
- It runs whether or not the per-turn learning loop (cognition.review_enabled) is on: the owner asked, as Hermes' manual /refine does.

Orchestrator.refine (agents/core/orchestrator.py:4252):
- It reads a snapshot of the session's history and never writes to it.
- The snapshot is conversation_snapshot (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:98): the newest turns whole and contiguous, each cut at 2,000 characters, up to 12,000 characters in all. Slash commands and the hub's replies to them are left out, so a chat of commands only has nothing to review. This replaces the per-turn review's last-6-turns, 300-character window for this path.
- In flight, as it really behaves: every path that dispatches /refine holds the session's turn lease first. A /refine sent while another turn runs therefore waits for that turn (up to the lease's 180-second bound) and then reviews the conversation as it stands; it is not refused (review-H465 m-1 corrected the earlier claim). The review itself is bounded at 150 seconds (REFINE_TIMEOUT_S), below that wait, so the chat is busy for at most that long.
- A direct caller holding no lease while another turn does is refused turn_in_flight: the lock is locked and the key is not among this context's held leases (agents/core/orchestrator.py:4277). No new in-flight set was added (critic note 1).
- A review's result is the reviewer's last_result, which GET /api/cognition/learning shows (reviewer.status()); a refusal does not overwrite it. Each action is logged.

The learning loop's knobs are declared settings (category learning, agents/core/settings_db.py:351): review_max_tokens (512, 1–32768), review_daily_budget (20, 0–1000), review_cadence (every_turn, every_n_turns, idle_gap), review_every_n (3), review_idle_gap_s (90) and review_max_facts (3), with the defaults the code already used, bounded in _LEARNING_INT_BOUNDS (agents/core/settings_db.py:956). The admin settings API, the HUD and nerva config set can change them; nerva config get shows a number named …max_tokens as the number it is, not masked as a credential, and masks every key the settings store encrypts (the GA4 service-account JSON among them), and nerva config set echoes such a value masked too (review-H465e nit 3). A model id is masked only under a hinted name: llm.default_model shows as typed. Every knob reads within its declared bounds whatever the stored row (a row from before the bounds, restored or hand-edited, reads as the default), the review's model call's token cap included (bounded_learning_int, agents/core/settings_db.py:975). A declared 0 for review_max_facts or review_idle_gap_s is honoured, not read as unset; corrections have a cap of their own (3), so a review_max_facts of 0 keeps no facts, still records corrections, and /refine says what it found but did not keep (_number, agents/core/learning/background_review.py:293).

BackgroundReviewer.run_on_demand (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:335):
- It skips the cadence gate but spends the daily budget, rolling over at midnight, and refunds it when no review was had (a model down, a cut-off answer, a timeout, a cancellation), on the day the pass spent it (review-H465f nit 1). A budget of 0 means no reviews and /refine says so (reviews_off); 2.5 reads as 2, and a value that is not a number or lies outside 0–1000 (text, infinity, a boolean, a hand-edited -3, a fraction below one) is logged once and 20 used (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:268). A per-turn pass that does not run leaves a DEBUG line naming why. It keeps the strict-local model, and is bounded at REFINE_TIMEOUT_S (150 s, below the lease's 180-second wait); no setting raises it.
- It neither resets nor delays the per-turn cadence. It runs one at a time and never beside a per-turn review: a /refine while a per-turn pass runs is refused busy, and a per-turn pass that would start while /refine runs is skipped, not deferred. The exclusion is taken in run() itself (agents/core/learning/background_review.py:394), so a per-turn pass spawned before the /refine, still waiting on the memory lock, is refused on_demand when it enters. A cancelled review leaves no busy flag.
- Its proposals, approval cards and new skills are labelled refine, not background_review; the label is passed down per pass, never kept on the instance. An injection-flagged correction is not recorded (on both paths). Facts found while living memory is off are counted after the injection scan, and said only to the owner who asked.
- run gains a focus slot in REVIEW_PROMPT ("Focus for this review: …", absent when there is none, so the per-turn prompt is byte-identical) and a context bound, which this path sets to the snapshot's.

Final review at HEAD 57ed6db (branch codex/hermes-progress-20261010). The Hermes `project` command tree is ported: create, list/ls, show, add-folder, remove-folder, rename, set-primary, use, archive, restore and bind-board (agents/core/kanban/cli_upstream/projects_commands.py:21-62), all dispatched against a durable per-profile store (agents/core/kanban/cli_upstream/projects_commands.py:236). The owner reaches it as `nerva project ...` (agents/cli/nerva.py:196, agents/cli/nerva.py:4891-4899), which posts to POST /api/kanban/projects/command (agents/core/routers/kanban.py:63-65). The store persists the active-project pointer (agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:633-640). Cards on a board bound to a project get a worktree under the repo and a deterministic branch name (agents/core/kanban/upstream/kanban_db.py:1285-1291, agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:734).

The one open gap was that the repo-discovery cache had no owner surface. That gap is now closed:
- Two new verbs are registered, `discover --depth N` (0-8, default 4) and `repos` (read-only) (agents/core/kanban/cli_upstream/projects_commands.py:63-67, agents/core/kanban/cli_upstream/projects_commands.py:417).
- `discover` walks the file roots breadth-first to find git repos. It does not follow symlinks, skips hidden and generated directories, and re-resolves every hit through the file scope. It has a directory budget, a repo budget and a per-directory entry budget, and reports when any of them truncates the scan (agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:775-819, agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:763-772). It then replaces the discovered_repos cache (agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:68-71, agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:838-847).
- The scan runs off the event loop via asyncio.to_thread (agents/core/kanban/projects_cli.py:108-111).
- The cache is keyed only by a digest of the file roots, and the scan depth is stored separately (agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:755-760, agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:90). The "cleared" message appears only when rows from other roots were actually dropped (agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:830).
- `repos` reads the cache without writing to it. If the roots have changed, it hides the old rows and reports them as stale instead of deleting them (agents/core/kanban/upstream/projects_db.py:850-866, agents/core/kanban/cli_upstream/projects_commands.py:400-409).

Tests:
- `discover` fills the cache: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:398
- Rows from old roots are hidden and kept until the next `discover`: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:435
- A non-default depth is listed and `repos --depth` is rejected: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:462
- The scan runs off the event loop: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:483
- The per-directory entry cap: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:518
- Owner-only access: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:531
- Scan budgets and scope: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:546
- The real `nerva project discover --depth 2` verb, then `repos` through the owner HTTP route; an unauthenticated call gets 401: tests/test_hermes_kanban_surfaces_wiring.py:164-193
- The project lifecycle: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py:24
- The store and discovery: tests/test_hermes_kanban_projects.py:264
- A board inheriting its project: tests/test_hermes_kanban_board_projects.py:31

Review history: the first revision (r1, bf7ba5e) drew reviewer findings. `repos` deleted rows and depended on depth, the scan blocked the event loop, and the first scan printed a "cleared" message. r2 fixed all three with tests written red-first, passed two adversarial skeptics, and was cherry-picked onto HEAD.

Honest limits:
- There is no desktop or web Projects view of the discovered repos. The owner surfaces are the CLI verb and the HTTP command route.
- On a roots change, `repos` reports the cache as stale rather than deleting it. The next `discover` replaces it.
- I did not run the guard suites myself; their 133 passes are the implementer's figure. Only the four row test files below were run here.

Test runs: tests/test_hermes_projects_cli.py, tests/test_hermes_kanban_projects.py, tests/test_hermes_kanban_board_projects.py and tests/test_hermes_kanban_surfaces_wiring.py were each run twice at HEAD. 2026-10-09 cloud standalone-image continuation: newly approved cloud PNGs now use the committed shared sidecar publisher and ID reservation. The generated-ID download/edit reader checks the expected digest, while local task recovery still independently checks the durable completion SHA. Cloud root safety remains checked before publication and at the final guard; live authority is rechecked immediately before the PNG link. Storage failures retain unknown outcome, governance declines after generation withhold, and machinery/mediation failures retain their existing classifications. Approval configuration binds the actual imported publisher source and refuses source drift. Existing completion/projection/catalog shapes and the single provider dispatch remain intact; restart recovery performs no request. The earlier local-only limit below is superseded for new built-in cloud artifacts; legacy sidecar-free IDs remain unbound on raw reads and no old artifact is backfilled. H477 remains partial. 2026-10-09 standalone local-image continuation: new ComfyUI and local OpenAI PNGs persist a strict expected-digest sidecar. The shared generated-ID reader verifies exactly its returned bytes for downloads and edit references, refusing malformed metadata or mismatch. Cooperating local publishers reserve an ID, refuse existing final names, sync private files, link the sidecar first and recheck authority immediately before the PNG link. Prepublication failure removes only this invocation's sidecar; after PNG publication or an ambiguous link outcome whose identity cannot be established, the binding stays. Directory sync is best effort, and missing sidecars preserve legacy availability without a verified claim. Separate cloud publication does not participate in this reservation; a forced same-ID mixed pair can refuse until reconciled, and deletion of metadata cannot be distinguished from legacy. The existing user guard, response shape and no-replay boundary remain intact. This increment does not close H477. 2026-10-09 local-producer continuation: the shared atomic PNG publisher now returns SHA-256 of its already-validated immutable bytes after successful publication. ComfyUI and local OpenAI image generation pass that producer digest through MediaGenManager to the optional catalog field without opening a result path. New catalog rows from these built-in producers therefore verify on md delivery/export; a same-size different valid PNG is refused. Missing producer hashes preserve legacy catalog calls, while present malformed values including null skip cataloging with the existing generation-success/warning behavior. The seven-file focused union passes 189 cases using offline actual-backend fixtures. Typed task artifact views and raw download enforcement remain unchanged; raw producer output gains the additive digest. This does not bind old rows or arbitrary legacy producers. 2026-10-09 expected-digest continuation: new cloud-completion catalog rows carry their verified completion SHA-256. Catalog delivery/export freezes one selected row for path and expected digest, reads bounded MIME-valid bytes and refuses a mismatch; exports mark bound rows verified and legacy rows unbound. Strict optional-field validation rejects malformed stored/supplied hashes. Stable-ID retries retain the existing row without silent hash migration or removal. No new network dispatch, ownership boundary or local-producer binding is added. reviews.summary: `nerva send` trimite un mesaj către o destinație configurată fără apel de model, cu corpul rezolvat ca la Hermes: argumentul MESSAGE, altfel `-f PATH` (`-` citește stdin), altfel ce e legat pe stdin — un terminal nu e citit niciodată, nici cu `-f -`; un stdin închis e eroare de utilizare, nu traceback; se citește cel mult limita plus un caracter, iar un BOM UTF-8 e eliminat. `-s LINE` e un subiect pe o singură linie *imprimabilă* (orice caracter de control sau separator de linie Unicode e refuzat), purtat de ntfy ca titlu nativ — ASCII imprimabil, cel mult 120, refuzat cu motiv în loc să fie trunchiat tacit de adaptor — și de celelalte canale ca prima linie (subiect, linie goală, mesaj — forma Hermes); `-q` nu tipărește nimic la succes; `--list CANAL` filtrează țintele: un nume care nu poate fi canal direct-send e eroare de utilizare decisă offline, iar un canal pe care un hub mai vechi nu-l listează e exit 1 cu ce listează numit; un argument MESSAGE gol înseamnă „fără mesaj” și cade pe `--file`/stdin. Scara de ieșire e declarată în `--help`: 0 trimis · 1 nelivrat (hub-ul a refuzat sau transportul a eșuat) · 2 utilizare · 3 fără hub · 4 neautorizat. Un fișier binar la `-f` e refuzat cu îndrumarea pentru atașamente, fără să-i reflecte octeții; limita de 4.000 de caractere e regula seam-ului (`carried_length`: subiectul contează unde devine prima linie, nu la ntfy) și CLI-ul aplică aceeași regulă înainte de orice cerere; șirurile venite de la hub sau tastate sunt curățate de caractere de control înainte de terminal. `POST /api/channels/send` primește `subject` opțional (o linie, ≤200), iar seam-ul outbound aplică limita la ce se livrează efectiv. Rate-limit-ul și înregistrarea în IntentLog rămân pe drum. O recenzie adversarială independentă a găsit cincisprezece probleme (două majore: două pin-uri existente din `tests/test_nerva_send.py` rupte), toate remediate în același PR, fiecare cu test. Nu există adresare `platform:chat_id[:thread]` / `platform:#canal` ca la Hermes: `--channel telegram` înseamnă întotdeauna chat-ul owner-ului. Precedența diverge deliberat: la Hermes argumentul câștigă în fața `--file`, aici ambele deodată e eroare de utilizare. Erorile nu au prefixul `hermes send:`. `JobRunner._send` își păstrează propria rezolvare a destinației (lot-ul jobs). Fără probă live pe un canal real din această sesiune: verificarea a fost prin hub fals și prin ChannelManager-ul real cu adaptoare false.

reviews.summary: **The variant-expansion half of the row.** `hardline_match` no longer screens one spelling: the old single-pass body becomes `_scan_one`, and the public function screens the command in every spelling `_detection_variants` yields — as given, unwrapped from a shell wrapper (`_shell_c_payloads`, recursively to `_MAX_SHELL_DEPTH = 2`), and de-obfuscated (intra-word quotes and escapes collapsed, so `mk""fs` reads as `mkfs`), type-preserving so an argv stays an argv. A non-string command is materialised ONCE up front, which fixes a real one-shot-iterator drain that turned `hardline_match(iter(["rm","-rf","/"]))` from a refusal into a miss. The original slice changed nothing in HARDLINE or the contract, so that pass was additive: an 80,000-case differential fuzz against the pre-slice module returned `refusals_cleared_by_slice = 0`. **That invariant no longer describes the module after PR #1177** (re-assessed 2026-09-19 against the diff 1c5054ea→494a13b2): HARDLINE itself changed — `_CMD` and `network_to_shell` now carry a `_PATH_PREFIX`, so a command word and any wrapper in front of it are read by basename (`/sbin/mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda`, `/usr/bin/sudo /sbin/mkfs.ext4`, `curl … | /bin/sh` all refuse where they returned None; `_recursive_root_removal` compares basenames through `_command_name` too, so `['/usr/local/bin/rm','-rf','/']` refuses instead of only the two literal `/bin/rm` spellings) — and #1177 clears refusals in BOTH directions. Two false-positive classes are cleared on purpose (a `case` label; a heredoc body that quotes a catastrophe), and #1177's mechanisms for them ALSO cleared TRUE refusals the pre-#1177 module gave — **both closed by this slice (H481, branch `hermes/h481-cleared-refusals`, 2026-09-22).** `_strip_case_labels` acted on the flat text of any `case…esac` span and its first-label rule fired after any word-initial `in`, so `(echo case in; reboot); echo esac` — which /bin/sh, dash and bash all execute — went `power_cycle`→None, and the `$IFS`-spliced `(echo case in; mkfs.ext4$IFS/dev/sda); echo esac` / `wipefs$IFS-a$IFS/dev/sda` went mkfs/wipefs→None; the strip now fires only inside a real command-position `case WORD in … esac` region (a `case` keyword, confirmed per match by `_in_command_position`), so all three refuse again — and, made symmetric, a single-line `case $1 in wipe) rm -rf / ;; esac` refuses through the segment path too while `case $1 in shutdown) echo bye ;; esac` still does not. `_heredoc_feeds_a_shell` looked only LEFT of `<<`, so `cat <<EOF | sh` / `rm -rf /` / `EOF` and `cat <<'EOF' >x.sh; sh x.sh` / `rm -rf /` / `EOF` went `recursive_root_removal`→None although both hand the body to a shell that runs it; it now also reads the heredoc's own pipeline stages AFTER the redirection and a file the body is written to that a shell later runs, so those refuse, while `bash <<EOF` and a heredoc written to a plain file (`cat > README.md <<'EOF'`) are unchanged. Each shape was reproduced against /bin/sh, /bin/dash and /bin/bash first (harmless `echo RAN` stand-ins) and pinned red-first. **An independent review of that closure found nine items — three blocking, three major, two minor, one nit — and all nine are fixed in the same branch, each reproduced against the three shells first:** (1) the rewritten `_heredoc_feeds_a_shell` counted a shell UPSTREAM of the heredoc's pipe stage (`bash -c echo | cat <<EOF` was `power_cycle` although every shell prints the literal body); (2) it took ANY word of a later shell statement as the run file (`cat > x.yaml <<'EOF'` / `shutdown: graceful` / `EOF` / `bash run.sh x.yaml` was `power_cycle` — the exact config case the heredoc-as-data rule exists for); (3) it read an `xargs`-reached shell as a consumer (`cat <<EOF | xargs -I{} sh -c 'rm -f {}'` with a `reboot.log` line was `power_cycle`; xargs hands lines to the shell as arguments); (4) `_in_command_position` read the compact `if true;then case $1 in` as the word `true;then`, skipped the strip and refused the label (`;then case` / `;do case` were `power_cycle`, label-only in every shell); (5) the new `_CASE_BLOCK_RE` (`\bcase\s+WORD\s+.*?\bin\b.*?\besac\b`) was super-linear on ordinary prose — 4000 chars of case/in prose 10 → 531 ms, eight argv items of it 0.28 → 128 s; (6) the redirect-target branch re-tokenised every later line for every heredoc — 400 `cat <<E >x` blocks in 4000 chars 25 → 2,471 ms, 33.6 KB 109 ms → 97.5 s; the first pass's '78.7 → 78.4 ms' held only for input with no `case` word and never entered that branch; (7) the named-shell file-exec claim was overstated: `(sh x.sh)`, `{ sh x.sh; }`, `if true; then sh x.sh; fi`, `cat x.sh | sh`, `sh -c '. x.sh'`, `. x.sh`, `source x.sh`, `tee x.sh <<EOF; sh x.sh` and a quoted `> "x.sh"` target all ran the body and returned None; (8) this row still said 'eleven across two reviews'; (9) the report said 11 items were red before the fix when 12 were, and the `case WORD in` tightening was pinned by nothing. Fixes: the consumer test looks only at the heredoc's own stage and the stages downstream of it, and a stage counts only when its shell reads its stdin as the script (`_interpreter_call`: a `-c` line, a file operand and an `xargs`-reached shell are data — unless the `-c` line itself launches a stdin-reading shell, so `bash -c sh <<EOF`, `sh -c 'eval "$(cat)"' <<EOF` and `sh -c '. /dev/stdin' <<EOF` still refuse, verified); the file test looks only at the operand a shell RUNS (`_script_runs`: `sh x`, `. x`, `source x`, the same behind `(`/`{`/`then`, a file piped into a stdin-reading shell, a `-c` line that runs it), collects `tee` operands and quoted targets, and the statement lines after a heredoc are tokenised once, lazily, shared across heredocs and decided last heredoc first; the `case` region is found by three single-purpose searches (`case WORD `, then the first `in`, then the first `esac`), each starting where the last stopped, and the keyword-before test accepts the compact `;then`/`;do`. A 671,995-case differential fuzz against origin/main (the suite's 275 pinned literals recombined with 14 statement prefixes, 10 suffixes, 17 heredoc heads, 13 pipe tails, 4 upstream stages, 18 same-line and 10 later-line follow-ups, plus 60,000 seeded-random recombinations) returns refusals_added = 55,059 and refusals_cleared = 22,304 — so the first pass's 'refusals_cleared = 0' is withdrawn, not restated. Every cleared case is explained by one of the two changed mechanisms and belongs to a class no shell executes, each verified with `echo RAN` stand-ins: 19,311 by the consumer rule — a heredoc redirected into a shell that carries its own script or `-c` line, or into `xargs sh` (`sh -c cat <<EOF`, `bash run.sh <<EOF`; main refused both, every shell prints the body) — and 2,993 by the command-position rule — `case` used as an ARGUMENT followed by `label) …` (`echo case $1 in`, `x=1 case …`, `sudo case …`: a parse error in every shell) or a `case … esac` quoted inside heredoc DATA, where main's unconditional strip put a `;` in place of `in label)` and so invented a command position the shell does not have (disabling main's strip makes every one of them None on main too). Every added refusal is explained by the same two mechanisms (33,619 consumer, 21,434 command position, 6 in garbage recombinations with unbalanced quotes reached through the de-obfuscated variant) and adds an executing shape of the kind pinned in the tests. Two false refusals main had are therefore cleared on purpose and pinned as such (`sh -c cat <<EOF`, `bash run.sh <<EOF`). The cleared classes are still cleared on purpose: a `case` label (`case $1 in shutdown) echo bye ;; esac` was `power_cycle`; `_strip_case_labels` drops the pattern inside `case … esac` while keeping the branch body a command position, so `case $1 in wipe) rm -rf / ;; esac` still refuses) and a heredoc body that merely quotes a catastrophe (`cat > README.md <<'EOF'` / `rm -rf / will destroy the box` / `EOF` was `recursive_root_removal` because `segments` ignored the body flag `text` honoured; a body line is now narrowed to its `$()`/backtick substitutions via `_substituted`, so `cat <<EOF` / `$(rm -rf /)` / `EOF` still refuses). **An independent review found two blocking majors and four false claims; all six are addressed here, and every one was reproduced against a real shell first.** **(1)** The payload was taken as the token immediately after the first `-c`-shaped flag, and the search then stopped — but a shell keeps parsing options until the first non-option operand. `/bin/sh -c -x 'echo RAN'` runs, and `sh -c -x 'mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda'`, `sh -c -- 'rm -rf /'`, `sh -c -e …`, `sh -c -u …` and `sudo sh -c -- 'wipefs -a /dev/sda'` all returned None. One decoy character defeated the entire mechanism, reachable end to end at the transport's spawn seam. The scan steps over options to the first operand now, `--` included. **(2)** A `sh -c` payload is a shell SCRIPT, and a newline separates statements exactly as `;` does — but the newline was squeezed into a space before segmentation, so nothing ever occupied a command position on line 2 and `sh -c 'echo hi` + newline + `mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda'` passed the floor. **Pressing Enter was the bypass.** Unquoted newlines are separators now, quote-aware so a newline inside a string literal stays data and ordinary prose is not screened as a command. #1177 closed the way that screening could be switched off again: any `<<` opened a heredoc and an unmatched delimiter swallowed every following line as body, so `grep "<<<<<<< HEAD" src/x.py` + newline + `mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda` returned None; `_heredoc_open` is now quote- and `$(( ))`-aware, skips `<<<` here-strings, and a delimiter that never comes back opens nothing. **(3)** `_CMD`'s command-position anchor learned four more shapes a shell steps over, each a live miss: a brace group (`{ mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda; }`), a compound-command keyword (`if true; then mkfs.ext4 …`), an assignment prefix (`FOO=1 mkfs.ext4 …`) and `env FOO=1 mkfs.ext4 …` — and, with #1177, a fifth: a directory prefix on the command word or on any wrapper before it, spelled as deterministic `component/` chunks with `=` excluded so `FOO=/sbin/mkfs.ext4` stays an assignment and `echo /sbin/mkfs.ext4` stays an argument. **(4)** `busybox` was named as a shell but not as a command-position wrapper, so `busybox mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda` — the standard shape on exactly the container targets this module says it keeps the floor on — walked straight through. Four documentation claims were corrected rather than left standing, including the one that said the known-gap list was complete (the first review found five entries missing from it; #1177's second review found six more — a re-expansion budget filled with decoys, a path in front of the command word, a `<<` that opens no heredoc, a heredoc a shell reads as a script, a heredoc body screened as argv, and a `case` label — so the docstring now says twenty-two across four reviews) and the one that said an over-matched flag shape can never clear a refusal (it could: `powershell /c -Command Stop-Computer` returned None where `powershell -Command Stop-Computer` refused — fixed by the same change as (1)). A test whose NAME promised a bound on work it never measured was renamed to what it actually pins, which is the opposite: that depth-3 nesting is a deliberate miss (`test_nesting_past_the_depth_cap_is_a_miss_and_that_is_the_pin`, still present and green). **#1177 also removed the only breadth cap:** `_MAX_SHELL_EXPANSIONS = 8` bounded how many level-1 payloads were unwrapped again, in encounter order — an order the caller writes — so eight cheap `sh -c ok;` decoys in front of `sh -c "sh -c 'mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda'"` returned None where seven refused, and padding a payload past `MAX_ARG_CHARS` had the same effect; every payload is now re-expanded and `_MAX_SHELL_DEPTH` is the only cap, with breadth bounded by the fact that each level's payloads are disjoint substrings of the level above. And the heredoc-as-data rule from the earlier review gained the exception it was missing: `bash <<EOF`, `sh <<'EOF'`, `bash -s <<EOF` and `cat x | sh <<EOF` hand the body to a shell that RUNS it, and `_heredoc_feeds_a_shell` now keeps those lines as statements (`bash <<EOF` / `mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda` / `EOF` was None). All 303 tests in tests/test_local_transport.py pass (up from 206 on the #1177 module: 18 items for the two closures and 54 from the review round, which pin eleven false-refusal shapes and three own-stage data shapes as None, fourteen file-exec spellings, seven payload-launched-shell shapes and four downstream stdin-reading shells as refusals, the compact `;then case` (four), the `case WORD in` opener, four disclosed gaps as still-misses, and six wall-clock bounds two orders of magnitude above the fixed cost; every fix was neutered once — thirteen mutations, each turning its test red). Measured 2026-09-22. **Second adversarial pass (2026-09-22, round two).** A bypass hunter ran 64 shapes under /bin/sh, /bin/dash and /bin/bash with a PATH-shim stand-in that touches a sentinel and found three the floor cleared while every shell (or bash alone) ran the body: a subshell as the final pipe stage with no `;` (`cat <<EOF | (sh)`, `( sh )`, `(exec sh)` — `_stage_words` left the trailing `)` and `_interpreter_call` read `sh` as running a script named `)`), a `<<<` here-string into a stdin-reading shell (`sh <<< reboot`, `cat <<< reboot | sh` — `_heredoc_open` skipped `<<<` as having no body and nothing modelled the WORD), and a heredoc opened inside a `<(...)` process substitution a leading `source`/shell runs (`source <(cat <<EOF …)`, `sh <(…)`). All three refuse now: `_stage_words` drops trailing group closers, `_herestring_scripts` screens a here-string WORD (dequoted) when its own or a downstream stage is a stdin shell, and `_heredoc_feeds_a_shell` gains the process-substitution case; each pinned red-first with the exact bytes. The `_detection_variants` disclosure that the pipe machinery "misses two more pipe shapes" was an undercount and is corrected; the six disclosed gaps that remain (bare `./x.sh`, a variable-carried name, `BASH_ENV`, a heredoc inside `$( )`, `xargs -I{} sh -c '{}'`, `| (cd /tmp; sh)`) were each confirmed to execute exactly as disclosed.

reviews.summary: Consecutive-denial breaker. The tally is one row per session, session instance and principal, kept in chat_guardian_denial_tallies and capped at the 256 most recently denied consumer keys (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2590-2628). The warning threshold is JARVIS_SMART_DENIAL_BREAKER_THRESHOLD, default 3, 0 = off (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:93-102). The tally has two feeders. The first is the opt-in smart reviewer's DENY verdict (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:3952-3954), and the reviewer only runs when JARVIS_SMART_APPROVALS is set (agents/core/autonomy/smart_approvals.py:76). The second, new in this change, is the owner's own refusal, so the breaker now works with default settings. _record_chat_owner_denial_locked counts one event per task, computed on the pre-decision row; a card the reviewer already denied and the owner then rejects is still one event (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2638-2655). It is called from three owner paths: a single-card reject of a blocked or deferred chat terminal call in transition_with_group (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2098-2100); every member of a grouped reject in reject_pending_group, which is how a model retrying one command lands (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2347-2349); and the 'deny' choice of decide_reusable_consent, one event per member. The consent choices 'session' and 'always' are owner approvals and reset the tally instead (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:3283-3286). A recorded owner accept or edit also resets it (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2093-2094 and agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2458-2459), as does a reviewer approve. When the outcome projection reads a settled task, _owner_rejected accepts a human reject or a consent deny as a denial without needing any reviewer opinion (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py:2658-2663). A defer, a reject on a task with no ready chat terminal association, and a reject from another principal's chat do not touch this chat's tally (tests/test_h485_denial_feedback_queue.py:517-528). What the model sees. At the threshold the next-turn outcome block carries the STOP notice, whose wording now says the denials came from the security reviewer or the owner (agents/core/approval_outcomes.py:21-25). Inside a turn, a gated call that produces an active breaker sets guardian_stopped and the loop continues with the tool list empty (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:1072-1075); if the model still asks for tools, the turn ends with that notice (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:938-940). Pinned by the queue tests (tests/test_h485_denial_feedback_queue.py:476-490, tests/test_h485_denial_feedback_queue.py:493-499, tests/test_h485_denial_feedback_queue.py:502-514), the grouped and consent-deny tests (tests/test_h486_owner_denial_paths.py:57-71, tests/test_h486_owner_denial_paths.py:75-87, tests/test_h486_owner_denial_paths.py:91-98, tests/test_h486_owner_denial_paths.py:103-119, tests/test_h486_owner_denial_paths.py:124-137) and an end-to-end chat run where three owner rejections trip the breaker with the smart reviewer off (tests/test_h485_denial_feedback_integration.py:106-141). Tool guardrails (unchanged): StallObserver warns on the second identical failure (agents/core/tool_loop_guardrails.py:166) and can halt at 8 same-tool failures (agents/core/tool_loop_guardrails.py:177), but halting is behind the off-by-default llm.tool_loop_stall_halt_enabled (agents/core/settings_db.py:232), so by default these are guidance only; a successful result byte-identical to an earlier one becomes a reference stub (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:1407). Per-turn ceilings. The generic per-tool cap is still off by default (agents/core/settings_db.py:228). New: llm.tool_loop_web_search_cap and llm.tool_loop_subagent_spawn_cap are seeded at 50 (0 = off) (agents/core/settings_db.py:230-231) and accept whole numbers from 0 to 10000 (agents/core/settings_db.py:1051-1052). The coordinator binds web_search to its setting (agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:1784). The runtime applies the stricter of the generic cap and the tool's own ceiling, and an unreadable value reads as the shipped 50, never as off (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:137-138 and agents/core/agent_runtime.py:1309-1331). Calls past the limit are counted per tool per turn and refused (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:1333-1349). Pinned by tests/test_h486_turn_ceilings.py:31-35, tests/test_h486_turn_ceilings.py:39-43 and tests/test_h486_turn_ceilings.py:113-125. So web searches now have a default 50-per-turn ceiling an owner can reach from the settings. Sub-agent spawns are NOT effectively capped per turn. The ceiling is a guard in SubAgentManager.spawn that refuses with turn_spawn_cap only when a tool-loop turn is bound (agents/core/subagents.py:548-551), fed by the setting (agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:2470-2473, agents/core/subagents.py:439-450; tests/test_h486_turn_ceilings.py:197-212). Nerva has no model-facing spawn tool: spawn is reached only from the /api/subagents/spawn route (agents/core/routers/mesh.py:300-301) and from the batch helper behind /api/subagents/batch (agents/core/subagents.py:671-673), both outside any tool-loop turn, so the guard cannot fire in production (tests/test_h486_turn_ceilings.py:253-265). Those routes are limited by the per-boot spawn budget plus the concurrency and depth caps instead. The kernel LoopDetector and its status and reset routes are as before. Operator notes are in docs/FLAGS.md:1478-1503. No live-provider run was done. Re-read 2026-10-24 (batch 4): owner rejections and consent denials now feed the denial breaker, the breaker notice names the owner, and the web-search ceiling ships on at 50.
reviews.remaining: 1) The sub-agent-spawn half of the 50-per-turn ceiling is only a dormant guard: Nerva has no model-facing spawn tool (SubAgentManager.spawn is reached only by the /api/subagents/spawn and /api/subagents/batch HTTP routes, outside any tool-loop turn), so llm.tool_loop_subagent_spawn_cap cannot fire in production; it matters only if a spawn tool is added, and no 50-per-turn spawn ceiling exists today. 2) When a per-turn ceiling trips, the tool loop ends the whole turn with the cap notice rather than letting the model carry on with other tools; this is the existing generic-cap behaviour, now on by default for web_search. 3) Approval expiry does not count toward the denial tally, and no test pins that. 4) The breaker counts only chat-originated terminal_run approval cards; owner rejections of other gated tools do not count. 5) Stall halting (8 same-tool failures) stays off by default behind llm.tool_loop_stall_halt_enabled, so by default the stall guardrails only warn.

reviews.summary: The logging half of the row, and only that half. `agents/core/security/log_redaction.py` adds `SecretRedactionFilter`, a `logging.Filter` that runs every record's message and its `args` through `SecretScanner.redact` before a handler can write it. The enable flag is snapshotted at import, so an agent-authored mid-session write to `JARVIS_LOG_REDACTION` cannot turn it off — Hermes's `_REDACT_ENABLED` rule, ported deliberately. A cheap length/substring pre-check runs before any regex (≈8.75 µs per clean record, ~1.9× faster than the full scan; the builder's report said 17.22 µs and ~2.1×, which did not reproduce and is corrected here). `setup_logging()` installs it. **Two majors found by an independent review and fixed before landing:** the module's own docstring tripped the AUD-14 raw-env-read ratchet — the prose contained a literal `os.environ[...]` subscript and the ratchet greps file text line by line, so `tests/test_o26_p2_env_config.py` was RED in the delivered tree; and `install_log_redaction()` walked only the root logger's handlers, while `uvicorn` and `uvicorn.access` set `propagate=False` and own theirs, so the production HTTP server's own access and error logs — the ones that carry an `Authorization` header — were structurally unreachable. `install_log_redaction_everywhere()` now covers every handler owned by any logger in `logging.Logger.manager`, and a test drives a real uvicorn `dictConfig` and asserts a key in an access line is masked. Three minors fixed with it: the length floor was defeated by an extra pattern whose NAME collided with a built-in (it now matches by regex SHAPE, one-to-one, and fails closed on any mismatch); an ordinary `%`-format bug was being swallowed into a bare `[redaction-unavailable]` instead of logging's loud diagnostic (now `[log-format-error]` with the message, args and exception, all scanned first); and the test fixture destroyed an ambient `JARVIS_LOG_FILE` for the rest of the session. 47 tests, each fix red-proofed by neutering it. **Follow-up in the same PR:** the blocking bandit gate flagged both swallowed exceptions as NEW findings. Only the filter's last-ditch blank was suppressed (`# nosec B110`, with its reason); `_cover`'s per-handler swallow became a counted, warned coverage figure and `_managed_loggers`' registry-walk failure became a warning, closing the gap this row disclosed. 52 tests at landing. **#1177 (2026-09-19) closed a log-integrity hole inside this same control, re-assessed here rather than refreshed:** the in-place path used to give up and flatten the record to `msg`/`()` whenever a secret straddled the boundary between the format string and an argument ("correctness beats shape"), and flattening is exactly what DELETES a uvicorn access line — `AccessFormatter` unpacks five `record.args`, raises on an empty tuple, and `Handler.handleError` swallows it. `password_assignment`'s `\s*[=:]\s*` jumps the space uvicorn's `'%s - "%s %s HTTP/%s" %d'` puts between the request path and `HTTP/`, so `/login?pwd=` is inert on its own — 11 characters, so the 10-char floor does not even apply; `password_assignment` needs at least six unquoted (four quoted) non-space characters after the separator and the bare argument has none — and a match once rendered: any unauthenticated client could erase its own access-log entry by appending `?pwd=` to a path. `SecretRedactionFilter._mask_joined_args` now replaces whole arguments — one at a time first, then cumulatively for a secret assembled from several — the cumulative pass can also mask an innocent argument that sits between two culprits (`"%s HTTP/%s and %s HTTP/%s"` with two `?pwd=` paths loses the `1.1` between them): over-redaction, never a leak, and the arity still holds — — until the re-rendered line is scanner-clean, keeping the tuple's arity, putting an argument back when its conversion refuses the mask (uvicorn's `%d` status code stays an int), and naming the mask after the pattern the scanner reports, `[REDACTED:straddling_secret]` when it cannot. Flattening survives only for a straddle no masking can clean, i.e. the secret sits in the format string itself (`pwd=%s`). Seven tests were added — four of them through uvicorn's real `dictConfig` plus `setup_logging()`, asserting the access line for `/login?pwd=`, `/admin?password=`, `/x?passwd:` and `/z?api_key="12345678` survives with the straddling text gone (three are `password_assignment` straddles; `/z?api_key="12345678` is `generic_api_key` matching `api_key="12345678 HTTP/1.1"`, the access line's own closing quote completing the quoted value) and the client, verb and status kept — and the earlier straddle test was inverted to assert `args == ("[REDACTED:anthropic_key]",)` instead of `()`. `agents/core/log.py` did not change and still installs the filter from `setup_logging()`. `tests/test_log_redaction.py` collects 64 tests, all green on 2026-09-19. Nothing in #1177 touches the other six paths the row names; the still-owed list below stands.
reviews.remaining: This is one of the row's seven paths. Hermes applies `redact.py` to logs, verbose output, tool output, approval prompts, gateway messages, transcripts and memory; this slice covers LOGS. Still owed, and the rationale calls them the part that matters most: the hash-chained audit DB (a `cat .env` from `terminal_run` still writes a live credential into an append-only log that by design cannot be edited), the decision-inbox approval card the owner reads on a phone, task payloads, terminal output, and the observability exports — which Hermes scrubs unconditionally with no knob, returning `[redaction-unavailable]` rather than raw text. Also absent: the second mask mode (a syntactically INVALID `«redacted:ghp_…»` sentinel for file reads, so an agent cannot write a masked-but-plausible key back and silently kill the credential), `code_file=True` sparing source constants, `_mask_control_split_tokens()` for tokens smuggled across ANSI/zero-width characters, and the shared `.env` basename list. The two silent-degradation paths named at review are now CLOSED, after the SAST gate forced the question: a handler whose `addFilter` fails is counted and published through `uncovered_handler_count()` and a warning naming how many handlers are writing unredacted, and a `loggerDict` walk that raises warns that coverage fell back to root-only. The one silent swallow left is the filter's own last-ditch blank (`# nosec B110`), where a `logging.Filter` that raises would take down the caller's log call and the scanner has already failed. `install_log_redaction()` remains exported although the `everywhere` variant is what production uses. **A later slice's full-suite run surfaced one more thing about this control, recorded here rather than fixed:** the scanner's `high_entropy_secret` pattern matches an ordinary filesystem path. Under `-n auto --dist loadfile` a warning naming a pytest tmp file arrived as `truncated: [REDACTED:high_entropy_secret].md`, which is what a real operator would see when a log line names a file with a long random-looking segment — a debuggability cost the module docstring already warns about in general terms, now with a concrete case. Separately, `setup_logging()` installs the filter on every handler of every logger and nothing took it back off, so every later test on the same xdist worker ran under a live redactor. The installer is PRODUCTION code, not the tests: `agents/run.py` calls `setup_logging()` at module level, so importing it installs the filter during pytest COLLECTION — before any fixture runs — and eight test files import it; `agents/web.py` calls it from the FastAPI lifespan, so any test that drives the app installs it again; five test files call it directly on top of that. There is no list of leaking files to fix. The cleanup therefore lives in `tests/conftest.py` as an autouse fixture that strips unconditionally BEFORE each test as well as after — a snapshot-and-restore fixture, which is what the two neighbouring isolation fixtures do and what this was first written as, treats a collection-time install as pre-existing and preserves it for the life of the worker. That version went green locally and RED in CI on exactly the test it was meant to fix. The first attempt at it matched by `isinstance` and silently did nothing: `agents/` is on `sys.path`, so `core.security.log_redaction` and `agents.core.security.log_redaction` are two module objects over this one file with two distinct `SecretRedactionFilter` classes, and the root handler was carrying the other one. The match is by class name now, and four paired tests pin both halves — including the alternate import path, which is the case the first attempt missed.

reviews.summary: **Gap (a) of four, plus the row's `chmod 0600 atomic writes` clause.** Both pairing credentials stop being written in the clear: `SenderPairing._code` becomes `_code_hash`, and each deeplink entry moves from being keyed by its raw token to being keyed by an opaque 8-byte id with the token's salted digest inside the entry. Verification hashes the candidate and `hmac.compare_digest`s two fixed-length hex digests, so neither the length nor any prefix of the stored credential leaks and the deeplink failure reasons stay indistinguishable. A one-time migration accepts a pre-H497 plaintext file, rehashes it in memory and rewrites it, preserving each link's channel, `created_at` and `expires_at` — an upgrade never locks the owner out nor resurrects a spent link (since H689 a migrated link that carries no install id is refused as other_install, so the owner mints a fresh identity-bound link instead). `_digest` encodes with `surrogatepass` so a lone surrogate (from a hand-edited store, or from the body of the one pairing route a stranger is meant to reach) misses instead of raising. `atomic_write_json` lands every JsonStore file owner-only. **The review found three false claims and all three are corrected — two of them by changing the code rather than the prose.** (1) The module docstring said the store "holds nothing that can pair anybody". True of a 192-bit deeplink token; **false of the pairing code**, which is whatever the owner typed: a four-digit code was recovered from the file by exhausting 10,000 candidates in **0.006 s** and then used to pair. The code is now stretched with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 240,000 rounds, `kdf` and `rounds` stored beside each digest so raising the count later cannot lock an owner out, and a record written by the first cut is upgraded in place on the next successful pair — the one moment the plaintext is in hand — while a FAILED guess leaves it untouched. The deeplink token stays on plain SHA-256, deliberately: `redeem_deeplink` hashes once per outstanding link, so a slow hash there is a CPU lever for any stranger sending `/start junk`, and at 192 bits there is nothing for stretching to buy. (2) The salt comment defended leaving the code unstretched by pointing at the store-wide guess budget — an ONLINE control held in memory, which has no bearing on an attacker who has read the file, the exact threat at-rest hashing answers. Rewritten to say what stretching does and does not promise. (3) `atomic_write_json` claimed its chmod-before-replace ordering left no readable window. It left a shorter one: `write_text` creates the tmp at `0o666 & ~umask` and the whole payload is in it before the chmod runs. The tmp is now created EMPTY through a descriptor opened 0600 and closed again (json_store.py:74) before the unchanged `Path.write_text` call at json_store.py:78 opens that existing file — a mode `write_text` leaves alone — so no byte of a pairing digest ever lands in a file whose mode the umask chose; pinned by a test that neutralises `os.chmod` and still requires 0600. **#1179 (adversarial wave two) touched only this row's test file; `pairing.py` and `json_store.py` are byte-identical to the #1171 state.** The review claimed every inbound `/start` costs 240k rounds outside any budget. It does not, for two reasons worth keeping apart. First, `/start` never reaches the code KDF at all: a Telegram `/start <payload>` is routed by `TelegramChannel._maybe_pair_deeplink` (agents/core/channels/telegram.py:1514-1552) to `redeem_deeplink`, which is one plain-SHA-256 `_digest` per outstanding link, and every other chat message reaches `gate_inbound` through `ChannelGateway.route` with `code=kwargs.get("pairing_code")` (agents/core/channels/gateway.py:92), a kwarg no channel in the tree ever sets — so the one path on which a stranger can spend a KDF run is `POST /api/channels/pairing/request`, the route the new test's docstring names (tests/test_pairing_secrets_at_rest.py:472). Second, on that path the KDF sits behind a budget: `_code_guess_budget_spent` (pairing.py:611) is store-wide and is consulted at pairing.py:597, BEFORE `_code_matches` at pairing.py:597, so a stranger rotating sender ids — the per-sender bucket is keyed on an id the caller chose — buys at most `_MAX_CODE_GUESSES_PER_WINDOW` = 10 KDF runs per 10-minute window however many ids they present, and a request presenting no code never reaches the KDF at all. `test_the_kdf_a_stranger_can_trigger_stays_inside_the_guess_budget` (tests/test_pairing_secrets_at_rest.py:469) now pins that by counting `_stretch` calls rather than timing them, so a slow CI box cannot fail it: 60 requests from 60 fresh ids → 10 runs with 50 turned away `rate_limited` (with the budget check removed it is 60 runs and 0 refusals — re-reproduced at this re-verification), and zero runs for a code-less request. That is the code-side counterpart of the deeplink decision above — the token stays unstretched because nothing budgets `redeem_deeplink`'s per-link compare; the code may be stretched because its compare sits behind one. Nothing in #1179's persona-scan (`agent.py`, `quarantine.py`) or MCP-stdio (`mcp/client.py`) work touches this row. **Second slice (2026-09-22) — one store per process, and the one-use claim made true for the deeplink path.** The module promised a deeplink is "one use, ever", and inside one instance it was; production held two. The orchestrator registers the long-lived `sender_pairing` (the gateway gates on it, the pairing router mints and revokes on it) and `TelegramChannel` was built in `web.py` without one, so `_maybe_pair_deeplink` opened a throwaway `SenderPairing()` per `/start <token>`. A `JsonStore` reads its file once and every save writes the whole in-memory state back, so the two were two stores, not two views of one: a token redeemed over Telegram was spent in the throwaway and still outstanding in the orchestrator's copy, whose next save — any save; a stranger knocking is enough — wrote it back to disk, where the next throwaway redeemed it again and paired a second sender. With a relocated data root the two did not even share a file (the registry spelled a cwd-relative `memory_logs/sender_pairing.json`, the throwaway used `data_path(...)`), so under `JARVIS_HOME` no link ever redeemed. Fixed by wiring, not by hardening the store: `TelegramChannel` takes `pairing=` and `web.py` passes `gateway.pairing`, the same object by identity; an adapter handed nothing refuses to pair rather than building one (same reply as a bad token, a warning naming the cause, the message still swallowed); the registry entry spells the path through `data_path("sender_pairing.json")`. Five tests in `tests/test_telegram_pairing_shared_store.py` pin the resurrection with two instances over one file as the premise, a spent link staying spent after the owner's store saves, `revoke_deeplinks()` reaching the live adapter, an un-wired channel building nothing, and the real lifespan handing the channel `orch.sender_pairing` under the data root; red-proofed against the unpatched sources. Drift re-read (2026-10-12): diffed pairing.py, gateway.py and web.py since 92c3eeb3, telegram.py since 4b7714f9 and the two drifted tests since their pinned merges; the code hashing and PBKDF2 stretching, the store-wide guess budget before the KDF, the 0600 temp file and the shared store handed to Telegram and Discord are unchanged, minting now refuses without an install identity and redemption refuses a link with no hub id, the gateway adds a pending-reply route that still checks pairing for workspace channels, citations were moved to their HEAD lines, the remaining text was corrected because the owner/user command split already exists (only whoami is missing), commands.py and its test were pinned, no lockout or generated code landed, and the 79 pinned tests pass. reviews.remaining: **The row names four hardening gaps; (a) is closed, (c) is closed for the deeplink path, (b) is open and (d) is half closed.** (c) *revocation reaching live adapters*: `revoke_deeplinks()` and `unpair()` now act on the one object the Telegram adapter redeems from and the gateway consults on every message, so there is no second copy for a link or an approval to survive in — pinned by `test_revoking_on_the_shared_store_reaches_the_live_telegram_adapter`. Slack and Discord have no deeplink path and gate through the same gateway instance. Still outstanding, from the row itself: (b) *no lockout after N failed attempts* — the row wants a 1 h lockout after 5 failed approvals, checked BEFORE the pending lookup so a code already in flight cannot be brute-forced past it; there is still only a rate limit and an in-memory guess budget, both of which reset on restart. (d) is half closed: the chat command registry does split owner and user tiers on channels — `_channel_principal` makes only a configured owner sender an admin principal and every ADMIN-tier command refuses anyone else with "owner command" (agents/core/commands.py:177-183) — so a paired stranger gets only the user-tier commands; still missing is the always-allowed floor's `whoami` (no such command exists), so the row's `{help, whoami}` floor is not met. **Unaddressed from the Hermes column:** pairing-code GENERATION (8 characters from a 32-char unambiguous alphabet via `secrets.choice`) and the code's 1 h TTL — the code here never expires; "max 3 pending per platform" (the store bounds 200 globally); "1 request per user per 10 min" (it is 5); `unauthorized_dm_behavior` treating inbox-shaped platforms differently from chat-shaped ones; and the ordered authorization union (allow-all flag → pairing approvals → per-platform allowlist → global allowlist → global allow-all → default DENY), which is still an ad-hoc sequence in `is_allowed`/`gate_inbound`. **Two honest limits of the second slice.** The store itself still has no defence against a second instance — the guarantee is one instance per process by construction, and the premise test says so in words. And an install that had relocated its data root (`JARVIS_HOME`) and paired senders through the HUD kept them in `<cwd>/memory_logs/sender_pairing.json`; the store now opens under the data root, so those senders are held once more until re-approved (the owner's allowlisted ids never lived in that file and are unaffected). **And the limit carried from the first slice.** Stretching is a work factor, not a wall: a four-digit code goes from milliseconds to minutes, an eight-character mixed-alphabet code becomes infeasible, and **nothing enforces a floor on what the owner types** — `PairingCodeBody` caps the length at 128 and sets no minimum — while generating the code for them, the row's own prescription, is not implemented.

reviews.summary:
Nerva now warns about a dangerous host posture, as Hermes does, on top of a network half that was already stronger. assert_safe_bind (agents/core/boot_guards.py) still refuses an unauthenticated non-loopback bind and prints the exact env vars that fix it, and GET /api/security/posture still reports the secrets backend, skill signing, sandbox isolation and guardrails honestly. agents/core/host_posture.py adds the host half: three read-only checks that never block and never change anything, each answering ok, warn or unknown (it could not tell, never a false green), with a reason, what it saw and the fix. check_root (agents/core/host_posture.py:71) warns when the process runs as root (euid 0) on any host, headless included, or elevated on Windows (IsUserAnAdmin). check_sshd (agents/core/host_posture.py:168) reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config the way sshd does (_SshdScan, agents/core/host_posture.py:120): Include files are read in place, relative paths from /etc/ssh, each pattern's hits in lexical order, at most 16 deep; Keyword value, Keyword=value and trailing comments are accepted and keywords and values are case-insensitive; the first PasswordAuthentication outside a Match block wins, so a drop-in Included at the top overrides the main file; a Match block (to the end of its file, an Include inside it conditional) never sets the global value but a Match block that turns passwords on warns too; an absent directive is the sshd default yes and warns; no sshd_config is ok; an unreadable file is unknown unless the answer was read elsewhere; an unrecognised value is unknown. check_container_storage (agents/core/host_posture.py:241) first decides whether this is a container and then finds the mount the data root (resolved through symlinks) lives on in /proc/self/mountinfo (parse_mountinfo, agents/core/host_posture.py:216, with its octal escapes, and mount_of, agents/core/host_posture.py:230, taking the longest containing mount point and the later of two stacked mounts): the container's own root filesystem or a tmpfs/ramfs warns, a volume or bind mount is ok, no mountinfo or no mount is unknown. The container decision (changed by H283) is no longer the check's own: with the default marker=True it calls host_identity.container_marker() (agents/core/host_posture.py:244-250, agents/core/host_identity.py:525), the one host detector the system prompt also uses. **`JARVIS_MCP_STDIO_ENV_BASELINE` flips from opt-in to default-on**, so a spawned stdio MCP server is handed the `STDIO_ENV_ALLOWLIST` baseline plus its own `env` instead of `os.environ.copy()` — API keys, tokens, proxies and every `JARVIS_*` setting withheld. A second flag, `JARVIS_MCP_STDIO_ALLOWED_ENV`, is the owner-reachable migration remedy: a comma-separated list of host variable names that pass the baseline even when `_SECRET_LIKE` matches them. `_merged_env()` emits one INFO line per connect counting host values the child does not receive, carrying **no variable name and no value**. `GET /api/admin/mcp` rows gain `env_baseline`. And Nerva's own WorldView MCP server is handed its `WORLDVIEW_API_URL`, which the flip would otherwise have silently replaced with the built-in `http://localhost:4000`. **The review found two blocking majors and four false claims; all six are addressed.** **(1)** `routers/mcp.py` asserted an invariant the code did not hold: the comment said a row that spawns no subprocess reports `None` "rather than a badge it has not earned" and enumerated two cases. A third exists and is the only one an owner can create today — `POST /api/admin/mcp` does no command validation, so a row with a whitespace-only command or a shell metacharacter persists, and `connect()` answers `unsafe_command` from `_command_argv()` **before** `create_subprocess_exec`.
